questions.stem: For comparison, sample SD and confidence are held fixed while n increases. What happens to a t mean interval's margin?
questions.explanation: Larger n reduces estimated SE and increases degrees of freedom.
choices: It increases because there are more observations.
It decreases as SE and the critical t value decrease.

questions.stem: Which change best addresses a poll that includes only frequent library users?
questions.explanation: Correcting coverage is more important than enlarging the same biased sample.
choices: Collect ten times as many frequent-user responses.

questions.stem: A service meets its deadline with probability 0.80. What is the probability of missing it?
questions.explanation: The complement has probability 1-0.80.

questions.stem: Using the reported quartiles, group A has Q1=3, Q3=9; group B has Q1=10, Q3=14. Which has greater IQR?
questions.explanation: Use the reported quartiles: the IQRs are 9-3=6 and 14-10=4. No choice of quartile algorithm is required.
choices: The larger median must determine the IQR.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: The sample is an unordered set of cables. Why count combinations rather than different orders of the same set?
questions.explanation: Unordered sampling treats permutations of the same selected set as one sample.
choices: Reordering the same selected cables does not create a new sample set.
Selection order determines whether a cable is faulty.
Every sample set has only one cable.

questions.stem: A game pays a prize of 8 and costs 3 to play. What is the net gain on that outcome?
questions.explanation: Net gain subtracts the fee from the prize.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: All individual waits lie between 2 and 14. A normal approximation gives a tiny chance that a mean is below 2. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: An average cannot fall below the minimum possible individual value.
choices: The observations must include negative waits.
The true sample mean can actually be below every observation.
It is approximation error outside the true support.
The normal model is exact at every tail.

questions.stem: An exponential model has mean wait 4 minutes. What is its SD?
questions.explanation: For an exponential distribution, mean and SD are both the reciprocal of the rate.

questions.stem: A late-job rate is 10% overall but 30% during storms. What does storm information do?
questions.explanation: Different conditional and overall rates indicate dependence in this model.
choices: It changes the estimated chance of lateness.
It establishes that every storm job is late.
It proves the events are independent.
It makes lateness impossible outside storms.

questions.stem: The mean waiting count is 4 trials. Must the first success occur by trial 4?
questions.explanation: A geometric distribution has no finite maximum waiting count.
choices: Yes; the mean is a deadline.
No; it must occur exactly on trial 5.

questions.stem: 400 people are sampled without replacement from 20,000. Does this meet the at-most-10% sample-fraction guideline?
questions.explanation: 400/20,000=0.02, within the stated guideline.
choices: Yes; any random sample meets it.

questions.stem: A frequency table lists 1 page for 8 jobs and 5 pages for 2 jobs. Why is (1+5)/2 inappropriate for mean pages per job?
questions.explanation: A per-job mean must weight values by their frequencies.
choices: It gives extra weight to 1-page jobs.
It ignores how often each value occurs.
It counts too many individual jobs.

questions.stem: The course's binomial normal approximation check requires np>5 and n(1-p)>5. For n=100, p=0.02, which judgment fits?
questions.explanation: Both expected-count requirements must hold.
choices: It fails because expected failures are 98.
It fails because expected successes are only 2.
It passes because p is positive.

questions.stem: Two datasets have identical five-number summaries. What follows?
questions.explanation: Five summary values do not determine all observations.
choices: They can still have different internal distributions.
Their sample sizes must be identical.

questions.stem: A value equals its distribution's mean. What is its z-score?
questions.explanation: Its deviation from the mean is zero.

questions.stem: Mean is 100, SD is 10, and the supplied 90th-percentile z is 1.28. What is the corresponding value?
questions.explanation: Return to original units with mean plus z times SD.

questions.stem: A continuous uniform model runs from 4 to 12. What is its mean?
questions.explanation: The mean is the midpoint of the support.

source.slide_title: The center of a uniform distribution

questions.stem: A random sample of 80 enrolled students reports 30% support for later hours. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.explanation: A sample result is evidence about a population, not an exact census result.
choices: 30% describes the sample and estimates population support.
Exactly 24 students in the entire college support later hours.
Exactly 30% of all students support later hours.

questions.stem: Two normal curves share SD but have different means. What is equal?
questions.explanation: A common SD gives identical shape and width; different means shift the curves.
choices: Their probabilities below every fixed cutoff.

questions.stem: How does no arrivals in the next 5 minutes relate to waiting more than 5 minutes for the next arrival?
questions.explanation: No event before the cutoff means the next event occurs after it.
choices: The first requires exactly one arrival.
They describe the same event, ignoring a zero-probability boundary.

questions.stem: Why does a t interval use a larger critical multiplier than z at small degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: The t reference distribution reflects additional variability from estimating SD.
choices: The observations must all be larger.
Estimating SD adds uncertainty reflected in heavier tails.
The population mean is random in the formula.

questions.stem: A bar graph of counts 98 and 100 starts its vertical axis at 97. What impression might it exaggerate?
questions.explanation: A truncated baseline can make a small count difference appear visually large.
choices: The size of the difference between the counts.

questions.stem: Which quantity describes how sample means vary from sample to sample?
questions.explanation: Standard error is the SD of a statistic's sampling distribution.
choices: The range of all individuals alone.

questions.stem: In 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, the 18 is replaced by 180. What happens?
questions.explanation: The middle position stays the same while the total increases greatly.
choices: The median increases more than the mean.
The mean increases; the median stays 3.

questions.stem: Using the same sample and method, confidence rises from 90% to 99%. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Higher coverage requires a larger critical multiplier and a wider interval.

questions.stem: A spinner has three colors occupying half, one quarter, and one quarter of its area. Why is assigning each color probability 1/3 inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Equally likely colors require equal chance, not merely three category names.
choices: A spinner cannot have three outcomes.

questions.stem: Game A pays 5 with certainty. Game B pays 0 or 10 with equal chance. What is true?
questions.explanation: Both means are 5, but only B varies from play to play.
choices: B has a larger expected payout.
They have equal expected payout; B has greater spread.

figure.alt: Game A has payout 5 with probability 1; Game B has payouts 0 and 10 with probability 0.5 each.

data.alt: Game A has payout 5 with probability 1; Game B has payouts 0 and 10 with probability 0.5 each.

questions.stem: There are 20 independent trials with p=0.3. What is the expected success count?
questions.explanation: The expected count is np=20 times 0.3.

questions.stem: Ten cables are sampled without replacement from 100,000. Why might binomial be a useful approximation?
questions.explanation: A tiny sampling fraction makes dependence weak, but the exact design remains hypergeometric.
choices: The small sample barely changes the population composition.
All samples have the same faulty count.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: Two reasonable quartile methods give upper outlier fences of 18 and 20 for the same dataset. One observation is 35. Which conclusion agrees with both methods?
questions.explanation: The value 35 is well above both reported fences, so choosing between these conventions does not change the flag. An outlier flag alone does not establish a recording error.
choices: The observation is not flagged under either method.
Only the method with fence 18 flags the observation.
The observation must be a recording error.
The observation is flagged as unusually high under both methods.

questions.stem: At a tree node, two exhaustive outgoing branch probabilities are 0.6 and 0.5. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Exhaustive alternative branches at a node must sum to 1.

figure.alt: A proposed tree node has two exhaustive outgoing branches labeled 0.6 and 0.5.

data.alt: A proposed tree node has two exhaustive outgoing branches labeled 0.6 and 0.5.

questions.stem: Both endpoints of a uniform model increase by 4. What happens to its mean and SD?
questions.explanation: A translation shifts location but preserves distances.
choices: SD rises by 4; mean stays unchanged.
Mean rises by 4; SD stays unchanged.

questions.stem: A model predicts 5% of items fall outside specifications. Among 200 items, how many are expected outside?
questions.explanation: Expected count is sample count times the modeled fraction, without a guarantee.

questions.stem: A count variable has expected value 0.4. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: An expectation is an average, not necessarily a possible individual value.
choices: A single session must contain 0.4 events.
Exactly 40% of sessions must contain one event.
Its long-run average can be 0.4 despite integer observations.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD.
choices: A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.

questions.stem: A printer study uses only one printer per paper type. Why is that weak evidence?
questions.explanation: Replication helps distinguish treatment effects from variation among units.
choices: Two observations guarantee a representative result.
Replication would eliminate all possible errors.
Paper type cannot affect printer performance.
Printer-specific differences may dominate the comparison.

questions.stem: One hundred valid 95% intervals are constructed in repeated sampling. Must exactly 95 cover the mean?
questions.explanation: A long-run proportion is not an exact finite-sample quota.
choices: Yes; the confidence level fixes that count.
Yes; any other count proves bias.
No; the coverage count itself can vary.

questions.stem: A researcher takes 1,000 samples of 25 packages and plots each sample mean. What does one plotted value represent?
questions.explanation: A sampling distribution records a statistic from each repeated sample.
choices: A population parameter that changes on each sample.
The mean of all 25,000 packages combined.

questions.stem: A spinner has three colors occupying half, one quarter, and one quarter of its area. Why is assigning each color probability 1/3 inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Equally likely colors require equal chance, not merely three category names.
choices: A spinner cannot have three outcomes.

questions.stem: A normal model has mean 20. What is P(X<20)?
questions.explanation: The symmetric center splits total area in half.

questions.stem: The sample is an unordered set of cables. Why count combinations rather than different orders of the same set?
questions.explanation: Unordered sampling treats permutations of the same selected set as one sample.
choices: Every sample set has only one cable.
Selection order determines whether a cable is faulty.
Reordering the same selected cables does not create a new sample set.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: For a continuous duration, how do P(X<6) and P(X<=6) compare?
questions.explanation: An individual boundary point has zero probability.
choices: They differ by the density height at 6.
The second is always twice the first.

questions.stem: A rate estimate rises from 40% to 45%. What is its increase in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Percentage-point difference subtracts the percentages directly, unlike relative percent increase.

questions.stem: Remove 100 from 1, 2, 3, 4, 100. What happens to the mean and median?
questions.explanation: The mean changes from 22 to 2.5; the median changes from 3 to 2.5.
choices: The median increases and mean stays unchanged.
Both decrease, with a much larger decrease in the mean.
The mean increases and median decreases.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: Histogram counts are 3 in [0,5), 7 in [5,10), and 2 in [10,15). How many values are below 10?
questions.explanation: The first two bins contain all values below 10.

questions.stem: A rare-event binomial count has n=1,000 and p=0.002. What mean would its Poisson approximation use?
questions.explanation: The approximating mean is np.

questions.stem: A is 6 above its mean with SD 3; B is 8 above its mean with SD 8. Which is more extreme above its group center?
questions.explanation: Their z-scores are 2 and 1.
choices: The larger raw difference always determines extremeness.

questions.stem: Why does a t interval use a larger critical multiplier than z at small degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: The t reference distribution reflects additional variability from estimating SD.
choices: The observations must all be larger.
Estimating SD adds uncertainty reflected in heavier tails.
The population mean is random in the formula.

questions.stem: Ten independent trials each have success probability 0.3. X counts successes. What makes a binomial model appropriate?
questions.explanation: Those experimental conditions define the binomial setting.
choices: The expected count is an integer.
Fixed trial count, two outcomes, independence, and constant success chance.

questions.stem: A proposed event probability is 1.15. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Probability measures a fraction of total chance and lies between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: A count variable has expected value 0.4. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: An expectation is an average, not necessarily a possible individual value.
choices: Its long-run average can be 0.4 despite integer observations.
A single session must contain 0.4 events.
Exactly 40% of sessions must contain one event.

questions.stem: Students are randomly invited, but only 15% respond. Which concern remains?
questions.explanation: Random invitation does not eliminate nonresponse bias.
choices: Low response proves every answer false.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A rectangular density covers 0 to 4 and is zero elsewhere. What height makes total area 1?
questions.explanation: Width times height must equal 1.

questions.stem: Individual masses have SD 20 g; means of 25 independent masses have SD 4 g. Which spread applies to one package?
questions.explanation: The individual distribution keeps its own SD; the mean uses a smaller SE.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: 40 of 100 sampled jobs succeed. What is the sample success proportion?
questions.explanation: Divide the success count by the sample size.

questions.stem: 400 people are sampled without replacement from 20,000. Does this meet the at-most-10% sample-fraction guideline?
questions.explanation: 400/20,000=0.02, within the stated guideline.
choices: Yes; any random sample meets it.

questions.stem: Categories in a bar graph are reordered alphabetically. What changes?
questions.explanation: Changing categorical order does not change the observations.
choices: The number of observations in each category.
The display order, but not category frequencies.

questions.stem: A dataset's standard deviation is zero. What must be true?
questions.explanation: Zero spread requires identical values, which need not be zero.

questions.stem: A box has 8 red and 2 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. What is the minimum red count?
questions.explanation: At most two drawn tokens can be blue, leaving at least three red.

questions.stem: Normal models have the same mean. For a fixed cutoff below that mean, which has the larger lower-tail probability?
questions.explanation: A wider curve places more area beyond a fixed cutoff away from its center.
choices: The model with the larger SD.
The model with the smaller SD.
The one with more recorded observations regardless of SD.

questions.stem: A sum distribution has mean 100 and SD 4. What total is 2 SD above its mean?
questions.explanation: Add two times the sum's SD to its mean.

source.slide_title: A specified distance for a sum

questions.stem: The numbers of pages in six jobs are 1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 5. Which statement about the mode is correct?
questions.explanation: The values 2 and 4 each occur twice, more often than any other value.
choices: The mode is 3, halfway between 2 and 4.

questions.stem: A variable has mean 20 and SD 4. What z-score corresponds to 12?
questions.explanation: The value is 8 below the mean, or -2 SD.

questions.stem: The model changes from U(0,10) to U(0,20). What happens to P(X<5)?
questions.explanation: The favorable interval retains width 5 while total support width doubles.

questions.stem: A fair coin gives 8 heads in 10 tosses. What follows?
questions.explanation: Long-run probability does not impose exact counts in short sequences.
choices: The coin's future head probability is now 0.8.
Fairness requires exactly 5 heads in every ten tosses.
The next two tosses must be tails.
Such a short-run imbalance can occur with a fair coin.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at ID 3 and takes every tenth ID. Which IDs appear first?
questions.explanation: Add ten to the starting ID at each selection.

questions.stem: A supplied probability table lists P(X=0),...,P(X=8). To find P(X<=2), which entries are needed?
questions.explanation: At most 2 is a cumulative event including all counts through 2.

questions.stem: To estimate a population mean with unknown population SD using a sample SD, which standard method fits?
questions.explanation: The t method accounts for estimating population SD.
choices: A proportion interval regardless of variable type.
A known-SD z interval treating s as known population SD.

questions.stem: A supplied normal table gives P(Z<1.2)=0.8849. What is P(Z>1.2)?
questions.explanation: Use the complement for the upper tail.

questions.stem: Two servers share one power supply. Why might independent failure events be a poor model?
questions.explanation: A shared influence can create dependence.
choices: A power failure can affect both servers together.

questions.stem: Someone claims mean > median is a universal proof that any dataset is right-skewed. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Shape and centers are related, but the ordering alone is not a universal shape theorem.
choices: It proves every observation exceeds the median.
It proves the dataset is normal.
It is a useful common pattern, not a universal characterization.

questions.stem: Why report a confidence interval instead of only a sample mean?
questions.explanation: An interval communicates estimation precision beyond a single point estimate.
choices: It guarantees the true mean is the midpoint.
It expresses uncertainty in estimating the population mean.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the first success on trial 4?
questions.explanation: The first three must fail and the fourth must succeed.

questions.stem: Independent sample size increases. What happens to spread in original units?
questions.explanation: Totals aggregate variation while averages divide the total by n.
choices: SD of sums rises; SE of averages falls.

questions.stem: An exponential arrival rate doubles. What happens to mean waiting time?
questions.explanation: Mean wait is the reciprocal of rate.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: An exact continuous duration has P(X=4)=0. Can a timer report 4 seconds?
questions.explanation: A rounded recorded value can have positive probability even though an exact point has zero area.
choices: Only if the density equals zero everywhere.
No; 4 seconds can never be recorded.
Yes; rounding collects a positive-width interval of exact values.
Only if the model becomes discrete before rounding.

questions.stem: A population proportion interval is 0.30 to 0.42. How should a proposed proportion 0.50 be described?
questions.explanation: Being outside this interval is evidence against compatibility, not an absolute impossibility statement.
choices: Compatible because 0.50 is a valid probability.
Proved impossible under every future sample.
Outside the interval and incompatible with this interval estimate.

figure.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

data.alt: A proportion interval 0.30 to 0.42 with proposed value 0.50 to its right.

questions.stem: A stemplot includes an empty stem 2 between stems 1 and 3. What does that show?
questions.explanation: An empty stem preserves a visible gap on the numerical scale.
choices: There are no values in the twenties.

questions.stem: An independent fair coin has just produced five tails. What is the chance of heads next?
questions.explanation: Past independent outcomes do not change the next toss probability.
choices: Greater than 1/2 because heads is due.
Less than 1/2 because tails is favored.

questions.stem: A game has negative expected net gain. Can a player still win money on one play?
questions.explanation: An average loss does not rule out individual wins.
choices: No; every outcome must lose money.
No; the largest prize must be negative.
Yes, if positive-gain outcomes have positive probability.
Only after the expected value changes.

questions.stem: Only 5% exceed cutoff k. Which percentile is k?
questions.explanation: The remaining 95% lies at or below the cutoff.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: All individual waits lie between 2 and 14. A normal approximation gives a tiny chance that a mean is below 2. How should this be interpreted?
questions.explanation: An average cannot fall below the minimum possible individual value.
choices: The observations must include negative waits.
It is approximation error outside the true support.
The true sample mean can actually be below every observation.
The normal model is exact at every tail.

questions.stem: Q1 is 8 and Q3 is 14. What does the interval 8 to 14 describe approximately?
questions.explanation: Quartiles bound approximately the middle 50%, with ties and conventions affecting exact counts.

questions.stem: A model describes the mass of one package. Is its SD automatically appropriate for the mean mass of 100 independent packages?
questions.explanation: Units can match while distributions and spreads differ.
choices: No; the average has less spread.
Yes; both are measured in grams.

questions.stem: A dataset has mean 8. One observation below 8 is removed. What happens to the mean of the remaining values?
questions.explanation: Removing a below-average observation raises the remaining average.

questions.stem: A machine's success chance steadily falls as it warms. Which binomial requirement is questionable?
questions.explanation: Changing trial probabilities undermine the common-p binomial model.

questions.stem: Population SD doubles while sample size stays fixed. What happens to SE?
questions.explanation: SE is proportional to population SD at fixed n.

questions.stem: A is 6 above its mean with SD 3; B is 8 above its mean with SD 8. Which is more extreme above its group center?
questions.explanation: Their z-scores are 2 and 1.
choices: The larger raw difference always determines extremeness.

questions.stem: A population contains 4 observations with a sum of squared deviations from its mean of 36. What is the population variance?
questions.explanation: Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by the population size: 36/4=9.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 2 blue tokens. After a red token is drawn and not replaced, what happens to the red chance on the next draw?
questions.explanation: Removing red reduces the red share of the remaining box.

questions.stem: A stemplot key says stem 2, leaf 5 means 25 KB. Stem 3 has leaves 0, 2, 2. Which values does it show?
questions.explanation: The key supplies place value and repeated leaves represent repeated observations.

questions.stem: A symmetric proportion interval is 0.20 to 0.30. What is the estimate and margin?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is 0.25 and half-width is 0.05.

questions.stem: A sample contains 100 observations, but population SD is unknown. Does large n make that SD known?
questions.explanation: A larger sample can improve an estimate but does not make the parameter known.
choices: No; it is still estimated from data.
No; the sample mean must also be unknown.
Yes; the sample SD becomes the population parameter by definition.
Yes; n>=30 makes population SD exact.

questions.stem: Under a constant errors-per-page Poisson model, document length doubles. What happens to the mean error count?
questions.explanation: At a fixed spatial rate, expected count is proportional to length.
choices: It becomes the square root of the original mean.

questions.stem: A U(0,10) sample has mean 5.4. Must the model be wrong?
questions.explanation: Sampling variation can produce means away from the theoretical center.
choices: Yes; all uniform values must equal 5.
No; any mean proves the model.
Yes; every sample must average exactly 5.
No; a sample mean can differ from the model mean.

questions.stem: An open voluntary poll has 50,000 replies and a very small calculated margin. What remains uncertain?
questions.explanation: A conventional sampling margin does not account for voluntary-response selection bias.
choices: Whether its respondents represent the target population.
Whether the calculated margin must be negative.

questions.stem: A fitted normal model predicts 2% above a cutoff, while a large observed dataset has 18% above it. What should be investigated?
questions.explanation: A large model-data discrepancy warrants checking fit and assumptions.
choices: Only the number of decimal places.
Whether the model fits the observed tail.
Whether observations should be changed to fit the model.

questions.stem: A Poisson count has mean 9. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Poisson variance equals the mean, so SD is its square root.

questions.stem: Two samples have the same observed mean above a claimed population mean and the same population SD, but sizes 25 and 100. Which mean is farther above in SE units?
questions.explanation: The larger sample has smaller SE, making the same absolute gap more SE units.
choices: The larger sample changes the claimed mean.

questions.stem: Tokens are replaced and mixed after each draw. Compared with leaving them out, what does replacement preserve?
questions.explanation: Replacement restores the composition before the next randomized draw.
choices: The original color probabilities on each independent draw.
The same token being selected every time.
A decreasing total number of tokens.

questions.stem: A rate is stated per hour but a cutoff is inserted as a number of minutes. What must be done before using the tail formula?
questions.explanation: The rate-time product must use matching units.
choices: Round the probability to an integer.
Express rate and cutoff in compatible time units.
Replace the cutoff with the mean.
Multiply both numbers by the sample size.

questions.stem: Exact wait times are replaced by short, medium, and long categories. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories retain rank information but lose exact numerical distances.
choices: The ordering of the three categories.
The exact differences between wait times.

questions.stem: Two services have mean wait 10 minutes, but SDs 1 and 6 minutes. What does the larger SD suggest?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation describes variation around a center, not an extra amount added to it.
choices: Waits vary more around the same mean.
The mean must actually be 16 minutes.
Every wait is six minutes longer.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: A student treats z=2 as a probability of 2. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Z-scores can exceed 1, while probabilities cannot.
choices: A normal model cannot have positive z-scores.
A z-score must be a percentage.
A standardized distance is not an area probability.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.
No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.

questions.stem: A model allows counts 0,1,2,... without a finite upper limit. Can it still be discrete?
questions.explanation: Discrete support can be infinite without forming a continuum.
choices: Yes; countably many separated values can be discrete.
No; all infinite possibilities are continuous.
No; a count must stop at 10.
Only if every count has equal probability.

questions.stem: Which design permits an exact binomial count model with independent randomized draws?
questions.explanation: Replacement and remixing preserve the same independent success chance.
choices: Drawing most of a small population without replacement.
Replacing and remixing each drawn token.
Drawing without replacement until the box is empty.

questions.skill_group: CLT assumptions, shape, and sampling quality
questions.stem: Only successful downloads are sampled to estimate duration for all attempts. Does a small SE remove that selection problem?
questions.explanation: A precise estimate can still target the wrong population because of biased coverage.
choices: No; precision does not correct selection bias.
No; SE must equal the mean.
Yes; enough successful downloads represent failures automatically.
Yes; a normal curve proves unbiased selection.

questions.stem: A strongly skewed variable is converted to z-scores. Does it become normal?
questions.explanation: A linear transformation preserves distributional shape.
choices: No; standardization shifts and rescales without removing skew.
Yes; subtracting the mean removes the tail.
Yes; every z-score distribution is standard normal.

questions.stem: A grader does not know which practice format each paper's author used. What problem does this reduce?
questions.explanation: Blinding the grader reduces assessment bias tied to treatment knowledge.
choices: Students being absent from the population.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What is the median number of pages?
What is the mean duration of jobs?
What is the SD of file sizes?
What fraction of jobs finish on time?

questions.stem: A fixed fee increases by 2 dollars. What happens to net-gain mean and SD?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a constant shifts all outcomes without changing their spread.
choices: Mean falls by 2; SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: A constant-rate process averages 0.5 requests per minute. What is the mean request count over 10 minutes?
questions.explanation: Expected count is rate times interval length.

questions.stem: A modified box plot marks 30 as a separate high outlier. Its upper whisker ends at 18. What does 18 represent?
questions.explanation: Modified whiskers end at observed nonoutlier values; the outlier remains part of the data.
choices: The largest observed value not flagged as an outlier.
The upper fence whether observed or not.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: The second has a larger mean.
They have equal means, but the second has more spread.

questions.stem: Someone claims mean > median is a universal proof that any dataset is right-skewed. What is the best response?
questions.explanation: Shape and centers are related, but the ordering alone is not a universal shape theorem.
choices: It proves the dataset is normal.
It is a useful common pattern, not a universal characterization.
It proves every observation exceeds the median.

questions.stem: Which quantity describes how sample means vary from sample to sample?
questions.explanation: Standard error is the SD of a statistic's sampling distribution.
choices: The range of all individuals alone.

questions.stem: Independent trials have p=0.25. What is the expected number of trials through first success?
questions.explanation: The geometric mean is 1/p.

questions.stem: Which change best addresses a poll that includes only frequent library users?
questions.explanation: Correcting coverage is more important than enlarging the same biased sample.
choices: Collect ten times as many frequent-user responses.

questions.stem: A wait is uniform from 0 to 12 minutes. What is P(3<X<6)?
questions.explanation: The interval occupies 3 of the support's 12 minutes.

questions.stem: One model is symmetric and bell-shaped; another has a long right tail and decreases from zero onward. Which pairing fits those shapes?
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry and exponential right-skew are distinct modeling features.

questions.stem: Two mutually exclusive events each have positive probability. Can they be independent?
questions.explanation: For positive-probability disjoint events, the intersection is zero but the product is positive.
choices: Only if their probabilities add to 1.
No; one occurring makes the other impossible.

questions.stem: For one normal model, P(X<40)=0.20 and P(X<60)=0.85. What is P(40<X<60)?
questions.explanation: Subtract cumulative lower-tail areas.

questions.stem: A one-sample t interval uses n=16. What degrees of freedom are used?
questions.explanation: A one-sample mean t method uses n-1 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: A college wants each academic program represented in a survey. Which plan best achieves that directly?
questions.explanation: Sampling within each program ensures representation from those groups.
choices: Select the first students entering one room.
Randomly sample students within every program.
Invite only students who previously complained.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: They have equal means, but the second has more spread.
The second has a larger mean.

questions.stem: The success chance improves after each failed attempt because the process learns. Why is a geometric model questionable?
questions.explanation: Geometric waiting assumes independent trials with a constant success chance.
choices: The success probability is not constant.

questions.stem: For a standard normal variable, compare P(Z<-1.4) and P(Z>1.4).
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry makes opposite equal-distance tails equal.

questions.stem: Waits are nonnegative. Is that sufficient to establish an exponential model?
questions.explanation: Support alone does not determine the density or a constant-rate process.
choices: No; the arrival process and distributional assumptions still need support.
Yes; every nonnegative variable is exponential.
No; exponential values must be negative.
Yes; nonnegative variables have equal mean and SD.

questions.stem: A frequency table lists 1 page for 8 jobs and 5 pages for 2 jobs. Why is (1+5)/2 inappropriate for mean pages per job?
questions.explanation: A per-job mean must weight values by their frequencies.
choices: It counts too many individual jobs.
It gives extra weight to 1-page jobs.
It ignores how often each value occurs.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: All items in a batch tend to be heavy or light together. What is questionable about sqrt(n) times individual SD for the total?
questions.explanation: Positive dependence can make total variation larger than the independent formula predicts.

questions.stem: Which expression computes P(X>0) for a nonnegative count X?
questions.explanation: Positive counts complement zero when negative counts are impossible.

questions.stem: Using the same sample and method, confidence rises from 90% to 99%. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Higher coverage requires a larger critical multiplier and a wider interval.

questions.stem: A Venn summary has 30 in A, including 8 in both A and B. How many are in A only?
questions.explanation: Remove the overlap from the total in A.

questions.stem: Which change best addresses a poll that includes only frequent library users?
questions.explanation: Correcting coverage is more important than enlarging the same biased sample.
choices: Collect ten times as many frequent-user responses.

questions.stem: Individual mean mass is 3 g. What is the expected total for 10 items?
questions.explanation: Expected totals add, though actual totals vary.

questions.stem: Sample SD is 6 minutes and n=9; sqrt(9)=3. What estimated SE is used?
questions.explanation: Estimated SE is s/sqrt(n) and retains the measurement units.

questions.stem: A fitted normal model predicts 2% above a cutoff, while a large observed dataset has 18% above it. What should be investigated?
questions.explanation: A large model-data discrepancy warrants checking fit and assumptions.
choices: Whether the model fits the observed tail.
Only the number of decimal places.
Whether observations should be changed to fit the model.

questions.stem: X counts failures in exactly 20 independent trials; Y counts arrivals during an hour with no fixed trial total. Which distinction matters?
questions.explanation: A fixed set of trials differs from event counts over an interval.
choices: X fits a binomial setting; Y may fit a Poisson setting if its assumptions hold.
Both must have the same maximum.

questions.stem: A box plot flags an unusually large print job. Which conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation: An outlier flag identifies unusual position under a rule, not its cause.
choices: The value must be deleted before any summary.
The rest of the data must be normal.
The job deserves investigation; the plot alone does not prove error.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: The second has a larger mean.
They have equal means, but the second has more spread.

questions.stem: A model predicts 5% of items fall outside specifications. Among 200 items, how many are expected outside?
questions.explanation: Expected count is sample count times the modeled fraction, without a guarantee.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 2 to 10. What can be said about P(X>12)?
questions.explanation: The event lies entirely outside the model's support.
choices: It is the density height at 12.

questions.stem: A table contains 5 students using both devices. What does this show about mutual exclusivity?
questions.explanation: An observed overlap rules out disjointness in the table.
choices: The two use events are not mutually exclusive.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A density is flat at height 2 over a half-unit interval and zero elsewhere. Is height 2 alone a problem?
questions.explanation: A density can exceed 1; probabilities are areas, and the full area here is 2 times 0.5.
choices: Yes; every density height must be at most 1.
No; its total area is 1, and height is not probability.
No; total area may be any positive number.

figure.alt: A rectangular density has height 2 from 0 to 0.5 and is zero outside.

data.alt: A rectangular density has height 2 from 0 to 0.5 and is zero outside.

questions.stem: Why use planning proportion 0.5 when no prior estimate is available?
questions.explanation: The largest Bernoulli variance is at p=0.5, so planning protects against smaller assumed variation.
choices: It maximizes p(1-p), giving a conservative required sample size.
It guarantees half the population has the trait.
It makes the sample unbiased automatically.
It minimizes all margins to zero.

questions.stem: Data are 0, 8, 9, 9, 10. Which center is lower?
questions.explanation: The isolated low value pulls the mean below the median of 9.

questions.stem: Individual mean mass is 3 g. What is the expected total for 10 items?
questions.explanation: Expected totals add, though actual totals vary.

questions.stem: A symmetric central normal interval contains 90%. How much area lies in each outside tail?
questions.explanation: The excluded 10% splits equally between the tails.

questions.stem: A selected student's name is removed before the next random draw. What changes?
questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement prevents repeats of the selected individual.
choices: Every remaining student becomes impossible to select.
That student cannot be selected again.
The same name must be selected next.

questions.stem: A supplied Poisson table gives P(X=0)=0.12. How is the probability of at least one found?
questions.explanation: At least one complements zero events.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What fraction of jobs finish on time?
What is the SD of file sizes?
What is the mean duration of jobs?
What is the median number of pages?

questions.stem: Probability is shifted from a low outcome to a higher outcome, with other probabilities unchanged. What happens to expected value?
questions.explanation: Giving more weight to a larger value raises the weighted mean.
choices: It must become the largest outcome.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: A database codes printer brands as 1, 2, and 3. Why would averaging these codes be misleading?
questions.explanation: Arithmetic on arbitrary labels does not describe a meaningful numerical quantity.
choices: Every numerical entry measures an amount.
The numbers are labels; recoding them could change the mean.
The largest code is always the most common brand.

questions.stem: A symmetric central normal interval contains 90%. How much area lies in each outside tail?
questions.explanation: The excluded 10% splits equally between the tails.

questions.stem: Which sequence gives the first success on trial 4?
questions.explanation: The first three must fail and the fourth must succeed.

questions.stem: An exponential waiting time has mean 5 minutes. What rate per minute matches it?
questions.explanation: Rate is the reciprocal of mean wait in consistent units.

source.slide_title: Converting a mean to a rate

questions.stem: Which interval approximates the discrete event X=45?
questions.explanation: The one-unit interval around 45 represents its discrete probability mass.

questions.stem: P(A)=0.4, P(B)=0.5, and P(A AND B)=0.2. Which check supports independence?
questions.explanation: Independence requires the joint probability to equal the product.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: A box plot flags an unusually large print job. Which conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation: An outlier flag identifies unusual position under a rule, not its cause.
choices: The rest of the data must be normal.
The job deserves investigation; the plot alone does not prove error.
The value must be deleted before any summary.

questions.stem: A normal model assigns 0.90 inside an accepted interval. What probability is outside it?
questions.explanation: Outside complements inside; without symmetry of the interval its tails need not be equal.

questions.stem: A proportion interval is 20% to 30%. Which conclusion matches the target?
questions.explanation: The target is a population yes/no percentage, not a numerical measurement mean.
choices: Exactly 25% of the sample must be successful.
Every individual has a value between 20 and 30.
The population percentage is estimated between 20% and 30%.
The mean duration is between 20 and 30 minutes.

questions.stem: Two datasets have identical five-number summaries. What follows?
questions.explanation: Five summary values do not determine all observations.
choices: Their sample sizes must be identical.
They can still have different internal distributions.

questions.stem: Histogram bins have unequal widths but equal counts. Why can equal raw-count bar heights mislead about concentration?
questions.explanation: With unequal widths, density scaling is needed for area to represent frequency fairly.
choices: Wider bins always contain smaller values.
Every histogram must be a time series.
The wider bin spreads its count over more numerical space.

questions.stem: A wait is uniform from 0 to 12 minutes. What is P(3<X<6)?
questions.explanation: The interval occupies 3 of the support's 12 minutes.

questions.stem: Two successes in four trials can occur in several orders. Why must all those orders be considered?
questions.explanation: A count aggregates several distinct trial sequences.
choices: Only the first successful order can occur.
Different orders are the same elementary outcome.
The count event includes every order with two successes.
The expected count is an order.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: SE is 4 at n=25. What is SE at n=100, with the same population SD and independence?
questions.explanation: Quadrupling n halves SE.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution of scores has mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Approximately what percentage of scores lies between 45 and 55?
questions.explanation: The interval extends one standard deviation on either side of the mean, so the empirical rule gives about 68%.

questions.stem: A normal model's SD doubles with mean fixed. What happens to its model IQR?
questions.explanation: Normal quartile distances scale with SD.

questions.stem: Among 200 recorded jobs, 30 were late. What does 30/200 describe?
questions.explanation: An empirical frequency summarizes observations and can estimate a probability.
choices: A guarantee that the next job is late.
The number of late jobs that must occur tomorrow.
The exact long-run probability under every possible condition.

questions.stem: A normal model has mean 50 and SD 2. Which interval contains about 99.7%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses three SD on each side.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 0 to 12. Given X>4, what is P(X>8)?
questions.explanation: The conditioned support is 4 to 12, with favorable part 8 to 12.

questions.stem: Categories in a bar graph are reordered alphabetically. What changes?
questions.explanation: Changing categorical order does not change the observations.
choices: The number of observations in each category.
The display order, but not category frequencies.

questions.stem: What does a 95% confidence procedure mean in repeated appropriate sampling?
questions.explanation: Confidence describes long-run coverage by the method.
choices: The sample mean equals the population mean 95% of the time.
95% of observations lie in every interval.
About 95% of intervals constructed this way contain the fixed population mean in the long run.
Every interval has 95% of its length below the mean.

questions.stem: A box has 8 red and 2 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. What is the minimum red count?
questions.explanation: At most two drawn tokens can be blue, leaving at least three red.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: For a normal distribution, how do Q1 and Q3 lie relative to the mean?
questions.explanation: Quartile cutoffs are symmetric about the normal center.
choices: They are equally distant on opposite sides.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: Which event is the complement of at least one failure in three trials?
questions.explanation: The only way to avoid any failure is to have none.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: A mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Which report matches its target?
questions.explanation: The reported target is the population mean, with confidence understood as procedure coverage.
choices: Exactly 95 of the next 100 durations will lie there.
The procedure estimates the population mean duration between 10 and 14 minutes.
The median is guaranteed to equal 12.
Every future duration will be between 10 and 14.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: A uniform interval centered at 10 doubles its width while keeping center 10. What happens?
questions.explanation: Uniform mean depends on midpoint; SD is proportional to width.

questions.stem: A systematic sample starts at ID 3 and takes every tenth ID. Which IDs appear first?
questions.explanation: Add ten to the starting ID at each selection.

questions.stem: A Poisson count has mean 9. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Poisson variance equals the mean, so SD is its square root.

questions.stem: A population has 2 faulty cables among 10; 8 are sampled without replacement. What sample information constrains the count?
questions.explanation: Finite-population availability sets both upper and lower support bounds.
choices: Only whether the count is odd.
Both available faulty cables and available nonfaulty cables.

questions.stem: From the same sample, a 90% and 99% mean interval are built with the same method. Which statement fits?
questions.explanation: Changing confidence changes the critical multiplier, not the observed estimate.
choices: The 99% interval is wider but has the same center.
The 99% interval has a different sample mean.

questions.stem: A service meets its deadline with probability 0.80. What is the probability of missing it?
questions.explanation: The complement has probability 1-0.80.

questions.stem: Sample size rises from 25 to 100 under unbiased independent sampling. What happens to the center of sample means?
questions.explanation: Sample size changes precision, not the expected sample-mean center.
choices: It stays at the population mean.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.
